# Tokenizen

> Open-source infrastructure for the seller side of the AI agent economy. The main project is Capacity Attest: after an x402 payment for metered capacity, the paying agent leaves a signed, factual record of what was actually delivered, so other agents can check a seller's history before paying.

Site language is Dutch. Source, package documentation and the specification are in a mix of Dutch and English. This file is English so agents can read it without translation.

## What Capacity Attest does

x402 lets one machine pay another per request, without a human. It proves money moved. It proves nothing about whether the seller delivered what was paid for. That gap is hardest for metered and duration-based resources (GPU-hours, storage over a month, bandwidth over a period), because delivery there is a claim about quantity and duration, not a single response payload you can hash.

After settlement, the paying agent signs a plain factual record: what was promised, what was delivered (yes, no, or partial), a hash of the evidence, and the settlement reference. It is appended to a public, per-seller, append-only history that anyone can read and verify offline.

Deliberately not included: no reputation score, no ranking, no trusted-seller badge, no on-chain anchoring, no escrow, no dispute process, no token of its own. A score needs someone to compute it, and whoever computes it becomes the thing worth attacking. A signed factual record avoids that question entirely.

## Honest status

New, but no longer unused. It has been run end to end against a real live paid endpoint with a real USDC payment on Base, that transaction and the resulting signed claim are public and reproducible. Two independent, unrelated projects have integrated against it: a downstream test suite that pins it as a dependency and verifies real claim digests (YE-YI7/asm-spec#18, merged), and a from-scratch, stdlib-only Python reimplementation of the verifier by a separate project (Tamga Protocol) that matches 7/7 on the published fixtures and is now a permanent regression check in their own package. See the credibility table on the package README for links.

## Links

- [Source code](https://github.com/holistis/tokenizen): monorepo, MIT-style open source, package lives in packages/capacity-attest
- [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/capacity-attest): `npm install capacity-attest`
- [MCP registry entry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io): registered as `io.github.holistis/capacity-attest`
- [Technical write-up](https://dev.to/holistis/x402-payments-prove-money-moved-they-dont-prove-you-got-what-you-paid-for-2doo): why the gap exists and how this fills it
- [Official sources and payment addresses](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/official-sources): the official repository, payment request, price and payment address of Bug Bounty Intelligence (5 USDC on Base through x402, address 0x015Eb036560216B3051339061FF68A207E0fe88f), and the command that checks them. Any other address given for it is not ours
- [Check. Pay. Prove.](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/check-pay-prove): one real AI-agent payment on Base mainnet, checked before, paid through x402 and proven from the chain, with the commands to repeat it, six numbers each with a place to check it, and the limits stated first
- [A signed receipt that cannot name its own payment](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/a-signed-receipt-that-cannot-name-its-own-payment): a live x402 receipt that verifies and still cannot say which payment it is about, the measured cause in the reference implementation, and the corrections that followed in public
- [733,203 attestations were taken back](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/733203-attestations-were-taken-back): a count of revocations across the three largest EAS indexers, showing that every revocation is an issuer withdrawing its own statement and the counterparty has no move at all
- [600 live x402 services, none signing a receipt](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/zero-of-600-x402-services-sign-a-receipt): a measured count of how many live x402 resources declare the offer-receipt extension, the commands to reproduce it, the limits of the number, and a live endpoint that does sign one
- [Nine ways to fake a delivery claim](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/nine-ways-to-fake-a-delivery-claim): nine independent designs for making buyer-signed claims harder to fake, each built and broken against the real code, and the structural reason none of them fully worked
- [The Hierarchy of Agent Trust](https://tokenizen.nl/en/notes/the-hierarchy-of-agent-trust): a plain-language story explaining why capacity-attest stops at evidence and deliberately never becomes a score or a judge

## How to use it

It is a Model Context Protocol server with two tools. `record_delivery` takes an already-signed delivery claim and appends it to the ledger, rejecting invalid signatures and duplicates. `get_delivery_history` takes a seller address and returns that seller's raw claims in chronological order, with no summary or score. Run it over stdio, for example via `npx capacity-attest`.

The claim is signed by the buyer, not the seller, because the buyer is the party that knows whether the thing arrived. Signatures are EIP-191 personal-sign over a content-addressed claim id, verifiable offline with any standard Ethereum library.
